newsitem.title: UK: LME nickel option vols rise, aluminium whipsaws.
newsitem.headline: LME nickel option vols rise, aluminium whipsaws.

text.p: Nickel volatilities jumped this week as underlying futures challenged the upside again, with upside $8,000 calls the focus of the market.
Nearby implied volatilites are up about four percentage points on the week with March at 30/34 percent this morning, dealers said.
"The highest we traded them was 32 (percent) but I suspect they've been a little higher than that," a trader at a market maker said.
"We saw some buying early today, but it seems to have died off a bit," he added.
Buying was seen in $8,000 calls for March and April as well as $7,900 strikes for June.
"It's not surprising to see vols move higher. Strikes at $8,500 have always been bid at 35 percent after the last big rally and now we've moved back towards that territory," he said.
In aluminium and copper, the options market saw some huge volumes this week.

In aluminium, volatilities were hit on Monday by more selling of strangles from the Far East, dipping to 15/17 percent on the nearbys. But later in the week a big tranche of puts were bought for nearby months.
LME data showed that about 46,000 lots of aluminium puts traded on Wednesday. "A lot of people were mystified that the turnover was so high," a trader said.

Some traders said this may be buying back of options by a big Korean player which had sold them several months ago. But others dismissed this theory, saying that volatilities would have moved more than they did.
One trader said the open interest figures did not rise significantly, possibly indicating the business was passed around several times.
At the money volatilities ended the week around 16.5/19.5 percent, with the curve very flat. Vols for 1998 were around 16/18.
"If the market does take off, we'll see the curve steepen, like 1995," one trader said, noting that at that time there was a 12-percentage point gap between nearby and long dates.
Despite the flat curve, vols were strike dependent, reflecting market makers' positions largely long on the downside and short the upside, traders said.

In copper, there was also some large volumes seen, but this was said to be transfers of European traded options to the new TAPOS contracts, not representing fresh business. "We think people are selling traded options and buying TAPOS, paying three quarters of a vol higher for TAPOS," a trader said.
Volatilities were little changed on the week, quoted around 19.5/22.5 percent for March, 19.75/21.5 for April.

"The market makers are a bit wary of marking up vols. They don't know whether there's going to be another wave of Korean selling," one trader said, referring to relentless granting of strangles in aluminium and copper since the New Year.

The $2,300 level, which has capped the three month price for weeks, was also significant in option open interest levels. LME data shows open interest at $2,300 calls of 1,161 lots in March, 1,475 lots in April and 1,850 lots in May. In July, $2,400 calls have 2,166 lots open interest.

Zinc options also saw some activity this week. Buyers were interested in $1,200 and $1,225 calls for May and June. Volatilities were about 1-1/2 percentage points higher on the week, quoted on Friday at 22/25.5 percent for March and 22/25 for April
As in aluminium, market makers are long the downside and short the upside.
"High strikes like $1,250, $1,300 are going to be very well bid, anything below the money not so much," a trader said.
There has not been a lot of producer hedging yet, one said.

"Most of the producers are waiting for the higher numbers, most of them don't want to think about hedging until $1,250, $1,300. But a few of them are scaling into it. There was a little bit a buying of $1,100s yesterday," one said.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
